## Where we left off

In Module 1 we fit models to a network we could **see** — every friendship in
`faux.magnolia.high`. Targets were easy:

```r
summary(fmh ~ edges + nodematch("Grade"))
```

::: {.lead}
Compute the summaries straight from the observed graph.
:::

::: notes
Recap in one breath: the intro had the whole adjacency matrix, so a "target" was
just a number we read off the network with `summary()`. Everything today is about
what happens when you *can't* do that.
:::

---

## The problem

Syringe-sharing among people who inject drugs is a **hidden network**.

- You cannot enumerate the population and map every tie
- Sharing is stigmatized, partnerships are transient
- There is no observed graph to run `summary()` on

::: {.punch}
So where do the targets come from?
:::

::: notes
This is the motivating gap. Unlike a classroom friendship survey, we can't observe
the PWID sharing network. What we *do* have is survey and meta-analytic summaries:
how many partners people report, and who shares with whom by sex, age, and race.
:::

---

## The resolution

ERGMs can be fit to **summary statistics**, not just an observed network.

```r
ergm(net ~ terms, target.stats = <numbers>)
```

- No adjacency matrix required
- The task reduces to: turn survey numbers into a correctly-ordered vector

::: {.punch}
"From aggregate summaries to network parameters" — that vector is the whole job of this module.
:::

::: notes
`target.stats` is the hinge of the workshop. Give ergm a set of numbers and it finds
the model whose expected statistics equal them. Our remaining work is translation:
survey summaries in, a target vector out. No fitting yet — that's Module 3.
:::

---

## Our population

```r
library(network); library(ergm); library(dplyr); library(readr); library(here)

nodes   <- read_csv(here("data", "synthetic", "nodes.csv"))
targets <- readRDS(here("data", "synthetic", "targets.rds"))

net <- network.initialize(nrow(nodes), directed = TRUE)
for (col in names(nodes)) net %v% col <- nodes[[col]]
```

n = 1,000 PWID with attributes: `sex`, `race.num`, `young`, `chicago`. The network
is **directed** — you name partners, and you get named.

::: notes
The nodes come from the HepCEP synthetic population. Attributes are the ingredients
for the mixing terms. Directedness matters from here on and is the first real
departure from the intro. (Footnote, only if asked: these summaries are prepared at
our n = 1,000 working scale so ERGMs converge live in the room — the scaling isn't a
lesson, just data prep.)
:::

---

## We don't count ties — we count partners

The survey gives a **degree distribution**: how many people report 0, 1, 2, …
partners. Directed, so two of them:

| degree | # people (in) | # people (out) |
|:------:|:-------------:|:--------------:|
| 0 | 646 | 606 |
| 1 | 203 | 202 |
| 2 |  83 |  93 |
| 3 |  37 |  46 |
| … |  …  |  …  |
| ≥8 | ~1 | ~4 |

::: notes
This is our population of 1,000. Most people name few or no partners; a thin tail
names many. That skew is the structure we want to preserve — and it returns in
Module 3 as the `idegree`/`odegree` targets.
:::

---

## Turn a degree distribution into an edge count

Every tie is one partner-slot for someone, so
**total ties = Σ (degree × # people at that degree)** — once for in, once for out.

```r
indeg  <- targets$indegree_data      # our population's in-degree distribution
outdeg <- targets$outdegree_data

inedges_target  <- sum(indeg$in_degree   * indeg$mean_n)     # 630.8
outedges_target <- sum(outdeg$out_degree * outdeg$mean_n)    # 791.5
```

::: notes
Pure bookkeeping — add up every partner-slot. No network required, just the
distribution. The two sums count the *same* edges from two directions.
:::

---

## Two estimates, one edge count → reconcile

In-ties and out-ties count the same edges, so they should agree. They don't —
`630.8` vs `791.5` — because they're separately estimated summaries, each with its
own error. Pragmatic fix: average.

```r
edges_target <- mean(c(inedges_target, outedges_target))     # 711
```

::: {.punch}
A target is a **count** — and the next step turns proportions *into* counts.
:::

::: notes
`711` is load-bearing: every mixing target is `edges_target × proportion`, so it
propagates through the whole vector. The in ≠ out gap is an honest preview —
summaries don't always reconcile, which is why simulation (Module 5), not the fit
object, is the real test of fit. (If asked about size/scale: the count and density
are size-dependent, but mean degree ≈ 0.71 and the mixing proportions are not — those
are what transfer across populations; Krivitsky, Handcock & Morris 2011.)
:::

---

## Homophily is one number. Mixing is a matrix.

The intro used `nodematch("Grade")` — a single count of within-group ties. But the
survey gives the **whole matrix** (from → to). For race:

| from \ to | White | Black | Hisp | Other |
|:---------:|:-----:|:-----:|:----:|:-----:|
| **White** | .76 | .09 | .11 | .04 |
| **Black** | .33 | .50 | .16 | .01 |
| **Hisp**  | .35 | .01 | .63 | .01 |
| **Other** | .64 | .11 | .20 | .05 |

::: {.punch}
Black → White = .33, but White → Black = .09 — an asymmetry `nodematch` cannot see.
:::

::: notes
`nodematch` sees only the diagonal, collapsed to one number. It can't tell that
Whites are strongly homophilous (.76) while Others barely are (.05), and it discards
every off-diagonal flow. Those between-group flows are where cross-community
transmission lives — for an epidemic model, the opposite of noise.
:::

---

## So we keep every cell: `nodemix`

```r
# intro:  one number  — within-group ties only
net ~ nodematch("race.num")

# here:   every from → to cell (reference cell dropped)
net ~ nodemix("race.num", levels2 = -1)
```

Sex (2 groups) → **3** targets. Race (4 groups) → **15** targets.
`levels2 = -1` drops the reference cell — the one all others are measured against.

::: notes
More cells = more faithful to the survey, but more parameters to fit. How you encode
mixing — one `nodematch`, `nodematch + nodefactor` for group activity, or full
`nodemix` — is itself a dial on model complexity. We reach for that dial in
Modules 3–4 when convergence gets hard; here we just note it exists.
:::

---

## Proportion → count: multiply by edges

The matrix gives *proportions*; `ergm` wants *counts*. The bridge is `edges_target`.
Sex, worked all the way through:

```r
M_to_M <- edges_target * 0.60 * 0.55   # 234.7
M_to_F <- edges_target * 0.60 * 0.44   # 187.7
F_to_M <- edges_target * 0.38 * 0.72   # 194.6
F_to_F <- edges_target * 0.38 * 0.28   #  75.7   <- reference cell
```

::: {.punch}
This is why the edge count mattered: no `edges_target`, no counts.
:::

::: notes
0.60 / 0.38 are the shares of ties sent by males / females; the second factor is the
within/between split. Four cells for a 2-group directed attribute.
:::

---

## The order is not the obvious one

`nodemix("sex", levels2 = -1)` expects the three cells in **`ergm`'s** order — not
reading order, not the order you typed:

```r
sex_target <- c(M_to_F, F_to_M, M_to_M)   # c(187.7, 194.6, 234.7)
#                 reference F_to_F is gone;  and M_to_F ≠ F_to_M
```

::: {.punch}
`ergm` matches numbers to terms **by position**. Swap `F→M` and `M→F` and you fit a wrong model — silently.
:::

::: notes
Two traps in one line. The reference cell (F→F) is dropped, so you have 3 numbers,
not 4. And because the network is directed, M→F (187.7) and F→M (194.6) are different
cells — swapping them produces a clean-looking, wrong fit with no warning.
:::

---

## Race: same idea, 15 cells — where it bites

Four groups, directed → 16 cells − 1 reference (White→White) = **15 targets**, each
`edges × share × mixing-fraction`:

| # | cell | target | | # | cell | target |
|:-:|:----:|:-----:|--|:-:|:----:|:-----:|
| 1 | Bl→Wh | 42.6 | | 8  | Wh→Hi | 46.6 |
| 2 | Hi→Wh | 41.7 | | 10 | Hi→Hi | 76.4 |
| 5 | Bl→Bl | 63.4 | | 15 | Ot→Ot | 1.1 |

**Do not hand-order these.** Read the order `ergm` wants off the labels:

```r
summary(net ~ nodemix("race.num", levels2 = -1))   # prints cells in ergm's order
```

::: {.punch}
Match your targets to *those* labels. Guessing the order is the most common way this pipeline goes silently wrong.
:::

::: notes
The reference here is White→White — a *different* cell than sex's reference, because
the reference is always the first cell in ergm's enumeration, which depends on the
factor's levels. That's the whole argument for never hand-ordering: let `summary()`
tell you the order and match labels to it.
:::

---

## The backstop: count your statistics

Labels are the discipline; the count-check is the seatbelt. It catches the most
common slip — a vector of the wrong **length**:

```r
f_mix <- net ~ edges +
  nodemix("sex",      levels2 = -1) +
  nodemix("young",    levels2 = -1) +
  nodemix("race.num", levels2 = -1)

target_vec <- c(edges_target,
                sex_target,
                targets$age_mixing_align_order,
                targets$target_race_num)

stopifnot(length(summary(f_mix)) == length(target_vec))   # 1 + 3 + 3 + 15 = 22
```

::: {.punch}
Length-match catches a wrong *count*, never a wrong *order*. Labels first, `stopifnot` last.
:::

::: notes
`summary(f_mix)` returns one statistic per term-cell in ergm's order; its length is
how many targets you owe. A mismatched length errors or silently recycles, so we stop
first. Ordering errors pass this check — which is exactly why the `summary()`-label
habit is the primary defense and this is only the backstop.
:::

---

## The vector is assembled → hand off

The whole job of this module: from a degree distribution and three mixing matrices to
one correctly-ordered vector of **22** target statistics.

```r
target_vec   # length 22: 1 edges + 3 sex + 3 age + 15 race
```

::: {.punch}
We have *parameters*, not yet a *model*. Module 3 fits an ERGM to these.
:::

::: notes
Everything downstream — fitting (Module 3), diagnosing failure (Module 4),
simulation-as-diagnostic (Module 5) — takes this vector as input. No network was ever
observed. That is the payoff of the workshop's title: aggregate summaries in, network
parameters out.
:::

1. Load `nodes.csv` and `targets.rds`; build the directed network
2. Recompute `edges_target` from the in- and out-degree distributions — do the two
   estimates agree?
3. Build `sex_target` from the mixing proportions and confirm its order against
   `summary(net ~ nodemix("sex", levels2 = -1))`
4. Assemble the full 22-length `target_vec` and pass the `stopifnot` count-check

::: notes
The exercise is the module in miniature: derive the edge count, build one mixing
block carefully, and assemble + check the whole vector. No fitting — that's next.
:::
